chapter_title: Chương 309: Dùng thị trường ra lệnh ban giám khảo

segments.title: Chương 309: Dùng thị trường ra lệnh ban giám khảo
segments.content:
Last summer, Beijing was dry with little rain, but this summer, there has been an exceptional amount of it.

After a torrential downpour, the temperature dropped a bit.

Taking advantage of the cool weather, Chen Guiliang and Bian Guanyue went up to the rooftop garden, cuddling and playing mobile games under the grape arbor. The only problem was the abundance of mosquitoes, which required lighting a mosquito coil.

Bian Guanyue leaned against Chen Guiliang's chest, just playing casually at first, but gradually her muscles tensed up, and her breathing became shallower and shallower.

In the end, she was even holding her breath, not daring to exhale.

"Ah!"

A terrifying scene suddenly appeared on screen, scaring Bian Guanyue so much she nearly jumped up.

Fortunately, she wasn't playing alone, otherwise she would have been too scared to even open her room door at home.

"This game is so scary!" Bian Guanyue complained after regaining her composure.

Chen Guiliang, however, was staring at the game on the phone, marveling at how brilliant the people at Dingguo Tech were.

The better the phone's performance, the more exquisite and smooth the graphics of "Seven Nights" became.

Achieving such an effect was extremely difficult.

A small workshop of seven people not only developed their own mobile 3D engine but also created a game with top-tier graphics and storyline. They had also completed testing on more than forty different phone models with just two to three hundred thousand yuan.

The phones used for testing were either second-hand ones from Huaqiangbei or borrowed from friends.

If Chen Guiliang hadn't invested money, Dingguo Tech would have run out of funds and released "Seven Nights" early after testing only 42 models.

Now, with Chen Guiliang's investment, Dingguo Tech had tested nearly a hundred models and even released patches to fix bugs on some of them. They had even tested it on Changhong and Bird phones.

The base version of this game was compatible with 70% of playable models currently on the market.

For the other 30% of special models, they had developed several exclusive version packages. When downloading, users could select and install the one corresponding to their phone.

The more powerful the phone, the stronger the graphical performance, making it a truly revolutionary work ahead of its time.

Its dynamic lighting and shadow effects, as well as its dynamic camera work, even crushed the contemporary blockbuster "Prince of Persia Mobile"!

The promotional articles Chen Guiliang had people write really weren't much of an exaggeration.

"Seven Nights" could run 3D scenes smoothly on a Nokia 5300 with 512KB of memory, which the judges at IMGA found incredible. They couldn't guess what clever techniques had been used.

And they were only a team of seven, with only a year and a half of development time, and on a limited budget, they were also developing another game, "Huangquan Road," simultaneously.

Chen Guiliang found it hard to imagine how they did it. He guessed that besides eating and sleeping, they were making games 24 hours a day.

But hard work and diligence alone weren't enough; they also needed a bunch of forward-thinking design concepts. This included their own methods for testing different phone models, which allowed them to do it quickly and at a low cost.

Bian Guanyue was now completely still, curled up in Chen Guiliang's arms and continuing to play, even forgetting that it was almost time for dinner.

"Huh, how did I get back to the first day again?" Bian Guanyue said with a puzzled expression.

Chen Guiliang smiled and said, "You reached the first ending. The protagonist doesn't dare to face his past and is forever trapped in an endless cycle of illusions."

Bian Guanyue asked, "So I failed the game?"

Chen Guiliang said, "You could say it's a failure, or you could say it's a personal choice. This is also an ending. There's nothing wrong with escaping reality; sometimes, facing oneself can be very painful."

"Oh, it's so late, and we haven't even eaten yet," Bian Guanyue said in surprise after checking the time.

Chen Guiliang said, "Let's go out to eat."

The two walked downstairs hand in hand and found a restaurant near their residential complex.

Even with Director Kou personally intervening, the GAPP ultimately did not approve "Seven Nights" for release, due to some bloody and horrific scenes.

But it didn't matter; the relevant regulations at the time were very vague.

Mobile games could be submitted to the GAPP, the Ministry of Culture, or the Ministry of Information Industry for review, but one could also argue that they weren't computer games and only needed to be filed with China Mobile and China Unicom.

Policies wouldn't begin to tighten until 2009, and mandatory review for mobile games wouldn't be enforced until 2016.

Cannes, France.

A group of judges were casting their votes. Currently, the vote for "Best 3D Game" was mainly centered around two games.

One was China's "Seven Nights."

The other was South Korea's "ONESEQUEL."

James Watson, editor-in-chief of the British publication *Mobile Games Insider*, said, "The so-called 3D in 'Seven Nights' is actually opportunistic. They use CPU soft-rendering to fake lighting and shadow effects, and it doesn't even support OpenGL ES. It's like putting a Rolls-Royce emblem on a bicycle."

Hans Berg, CTO of Deutsche Telekom's business division, chimed in, "That's right. South Korea's 'ONESEQUEL' is what represents true 3D technology in mobile gaming."

Ian MacLeod, former creative director at EA Mobile, retorted, "'ONESEQUEL' has terrible market prospects. It only supports high-end models with GPUs. Such high-end phones have a market share of only 0.3%. Is this game made exclusively for the rich?"

Ian slammed the table and continued, "Ladies and gentlemen, the Koreans' gaming technology is indeed orthodox and of a very high level. But 'Seven Nights' uses a self-developed 3D engine that enables 3D game scenes on all phone models. Regardless of whether it's pseudo-3D, the fact that it can achieve full model coverage is a huge boost to the promotion of mobile games worldwide!"

James Watson said, "We are discussing who to give the award to, not market promotion."

Ian countered, "What was the original purpose of establishing the IMGA? Wasn't one of its goals to promote the development of mobile games? A game that can cover all models versus a game that covers 0.3% of models—which one is more suitable for this award?"

Lee Jong-ho from Samsung's Mobile Game Partnership Department said, "Who the award goes to should still depend more on technical skill and game graphics. Even considering the market, 'ONESEQUEL' uses a commercial engine that all global manufacturers can follow, which is beneficial to the development of the global mobile game industry. But 'Seven Nights' uses a self-developed engine. If they don't make the engine public, how can other manufacturers follow suit?"

Jacques Dupont, a game consultant from Ubisoft's mobile division in France, said, "Other manufacturers can also discuss and study the technical solution of 'Seven Nights'. If the Chinese can do it, other manufacturers around the world certainly can too. Giving the award to 'Seven Nights' will promote the diversified development of mobile game technology, rather than having everything follow the current technical route."

Maria Lopez from the Barcelona Game Lab in Spain, however, was a proponent of the player experience.

She said, "'ONESEQUEL' is a cover-based shooter. There are many similar games, and I've become numb to them. It has absolutely no creativity to speak of, just a pure showcase of technology. They've even piled on so much tech that only high-end phones can run it."

"While playing 'ONESEQUEL,' I felt no anticipation. After finishing the game, I had no memorable moments. But 'Seven Nights' left a deep impression on me! While I was playing 'Seven Nights,' my nerves were constantly on edge, always trying to predict what would happen next. After finishing the game, I still remembered the plot of 'Seven Nights' and began to reflect philosophically on life."

"'Seven Nights' has achieved a perfect balance of technology, business, and art. Should a person bravely face their past, or just escape reality and live the same day over and over? The creators of this game are incredible, and I look forward to meeting them."

Rajiv Singh, from India, surprisingly also spoke up for the Chinese game. He took out a high-end phone and said, "My phone is already very expensive, but when I played 'ONESEQUEL,' it overheated and crashed twice. This Korean game is too demanding on phone specs. My gaming experience was very poor!"

The Korean, Lee Jong-ho, said, "That's a problem with your phone. A high-end Samsung phone wouldn't overheat and crash."

Rajiv Singh retorted, "Really? How come I saw you restart the game halfway through yesterday?"

Lee Jong-ho said, "That's because I was playing badly and wanted to start over. We are judging mobile games right now, not mobile phones. The quality of the game itself has nothing to do with how many models can run it! Mobile phone technology is constantly evolving. 'ONESEQUEL' can only be played on 0.3% of models this year, but that could become 30% next year. We can't just look at the present; we should place more importance on future progress."

There were a total of nine judges, from all over the world.

They argued endlessly over who should receive the award for Best 3D Game.

Finally, someone said, "Let's vote."

Just then, there was a knock on the door.

The vote was suspended for an impromptu meeting, because people from UOK had arrived.
